en: Because they produce delusion and because they manifest objects through the application of distinctions such as "woman" or "man," how are the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) like a plantain tree? They are like a mass of foam and so forth.
It is as follows: "A man with eyes" refers to the noble disciple;
"the sharp axe" is the weapon of wisdom;
and "entering the forest" refers to the people caught within the five realms of existence.
Because of the various doctrines of self and suffering, the plantain trunk is analogous to a tree;
[the view that] "it is new and straight" is the perception of a self as an agent and an enjoyer.
One should cut that down from the root by abandoning the perception of a self.

One should tear apart the leaf-scroll by means of the thorough investigation that it is merely the ripening of various volitional formations (*cetanā-saṃskāra*). Therein, one would not find even a mere pith, because those [formations] do not persist over time. How much less, then, could one find an essence? And how much less could one perceive a permanent self as an agent or an enjoyer, which is utterly signless? How is consciousness like an illusion? "Illusion-maker" is a designation for consciousness that has approached merit, demerit, and the imperturbable (*āniñjya*). "Standing at the crossroads of the four great paths" means being established upon the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*). "The fourfold work of illusion" refers to how, for example, herds of elephants and so forth are seen there; yet there is no actual perfection (*pariniṣpatti*) of those bodies of elephants and so on. In the same way, that consciousness—having approached merit, demerit, and the imperturbable and being established upon the four stations of consciousness—manifests an individual existence (*ātmabhāva*) such as that of the hells and so forth; yet there is no perfection of that individual existence by means of that [consciousness] itself. ... [This is called] the "perfection of the self."
The white synonyms are completed.
Oṃ.
The summary verse:
Birth, old age, and death; attachment, the state of being afflicted by defilements;
the expansion of passion, hatred, and delusion; and the distinction of the lineage.
Birth; lineage; caste; genus.

Birth (*jāti*) is, first of all, the connection of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhibandha*), the stage of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Birth (*saṃjāti*) is the completion of the embryo in the womb. Descent (*avakrānti*) is the emergence from the womb. Manifestation (*abhinirvṛtti*) is the period from the stage of infancy up to the stages of youth and middle age. Appearance (*prādurbhāva*) lasts until the stage of old age. The acquisition of the aggregates (*skandhapratilambha*) is the stage of name-and-form. The acquisition of the elements (*dhātupratilambha*) is the acquisition of their seeds within that very same state. The acquisition of the sense bases (*āyatanapratilambha*) is the fulfillment of the six sense bases through the growth of name-and-form. The manifestation of the aggregates (*skandhābhinirvṛtti*) begins from descent [into the womb] and continues until decrepitude. The appearance of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is the relinquishing of the previous homogeneous group (*nikāyasabhāga*) and the grasping of a new homogeneous group.
Old age consists of baldness and the tottering and falling of one who has reached the state of full maturity;
it includes the graying of hair and body hair, which results from their turning white and golden in color.

Abundance of wrinkles is the contraction of the skin. Senility is that paleness and loss of luster characteristic only of one whose age is fully matured. Brokenness is the state of having failed strength, power, and prowess.
The state of being hunched like a curved rafter; the state of having a body bent forward; the state of leaning on a staff;
and the state of having limbs covered with moles.
The limbs are variegated by lumps of time;
there is slowness regarding duties to be performed, such as standing or walking;
and there is dullness, which is the lack of proficiency of the sense faculties toward their objects.
*Hāni* (decline) is the lack of abundance in mindfulness, intelligence, and so forth.
*Parihāṇi* (loss) is the diminution of these very faculties and so on, following the passing of moments, instants, and the like.
*Indriyāṇāṃ paripākaḥ* (the maturation of the faculties) is the deterioration of those very same faculties.
The aging of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is the state of becoming ancient, the passage of time for the bases of the sense faculties (*indriyādhiṣṭhāna*),
and their state of decay; death is their transformation into something else.
Death (*cyuti*) is the relinquishing of the body;
passing away (*cyavanatā*) is the state of being in the process of dying; dissolution (*bheda*) is that wherein the physical aggregate remains as a corpse.
Wherein disappearance does not abide.
Furthermore, there is the dissolution of the form-body (*rūpakāya*),
the disappearance of the name-body (*nāmakāya*),
and the decline of vitality (*āyus*) and heat (*ūṣman*); these are maintained at the location of the heart at the moment of one who is dying.
The cessation of the life-faculty is the exhaustion of all vitality.
Death is the relinquishing of consciousness from the region of the heart.
The completion of the time [of death] occurs after that, whether one day has passed since dying, or two, three, or seven days have passed.
The six sense bases are non-attached; yet all foolish ordinary people become attached through the grasping of a self,
and they become thoroughly attached through the grasping of a self.

They are overwhelmed by various worldly views rooted in the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which are governed by the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*) and consist of the discursive movements of craving (*tṛṣṇāvicarita*). They relish the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) that are conducive to pleasant feeling with attachment;
they reject those conducive to painful feeling with aversion.
that which is conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

They approach [the six sense bases] with delusion; they adhere to the past six sense bases with longing; they dwell upon the future with delight; they become attached to the present with intense application; they grasp as "mine" the six sense bases belonging to others and included within their own appropriation. Based on the various forms of pride, they conceive of the inferior, mediocre, or superior six sense bases belonging to others as being part of their own appropriation. Regarding those on the level of non-concentration associated with the desire realm, they long for higher and higher states. Regarding those on the level of concentration associated with the form and formless realms, they solidify them according to their possibility because of the loftiness of their vital energy. Regarding the six sense bases based on the side of householders—consisting of forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles—they make them "flavorful" because they follow after the accompaniment of taste. Regarding the six sense bases based on the side of renunciants, through the application of laziness and negligence, they completely cast them aside.

In brief, these four terms—*iṣṭam*, *iṣṭam*, *kāntam*, and *priyam*—should be understood as indicators of a desired object (*abhipretavastu*). Furthermore, that desired object is, in brief, of three kinds: that which is to be sought (*eṣaṇīya*), that which is to be reflected upon (*vitarkanīya*), and that which is to be adhered to (*adhyavasanīya*). Among these, a future desired object is "sought" (*iṣṭam*) because it is being sought; a past desired object is "loved" (*kāntam*) because it was desired and merely wished for; and a present desired object is twofold: the objective thing (*viṣayavastu*) and the experienced thing (*anubhavavastu*). Therein, whatever objective thing is desired is "dear" (*priyam*); whereas whatever experienced thing is desired is "agreeable" (*manāpam*). Such is the extent of a desired object—whether past, future, or present, whether an object or an experience—that one might seek, reflect upon, or adhere to. All of this is expressed by these terms.

It is "desired" (*iṣṭa*) with reference to the future time, because it is to be sought after; "lovely" (*kānta*) with reference to the present time, because one who is not yet satiated desires it; "agreeable" (*manāpa*) with reference to the past time, because one speaks of it as agreeable when recollecting it; and "of a pleasing form" (*priyarūpa*) with reference to that which is beautiful, [pertaining] to the three times...
